blocks.content: PART A: BANK – CONCEPT, ROLE AND NEED

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Commercial banks serve as financial intermediaries by accepting deposits and lending money as primary functions.
Secondary bank functions are categorized into agency functions (acting on behalf of clients) and general utility functions.
Credit creation is a primary process through which commercial banks expand the money supply subject to statutory limitations.
The Indian banking sector consists of diverse institutions including Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), and Cooperative Banks.
Bank nationalisation in India was aimed at expanding credit access to priority sectors and promoting balanced economic development.

blocks.content: 1. Bank: Conceptual Meaning

A bank is a financial institution which performs the most crucial economic function of mobilising savings and allocating them to productive uses. It accepts deposits from individuals, households, firms and institutions who have surplus funds, and provides loans and credit to those who require funds for consumption, trade, agriculture, industry and services.
By performing this role, banks ensure that idle savings are converted into productive investment. Thus, banks are essential for economic growth, employment generation and development.
2. Banking: Meaning and Scope

Banking refers to the entire system, process and business activities carried out by banks. It includes accepting deposits, lending money, transfer of funds, creation of credit, payment and settlement services, remittances, and financial support to the economy.
PART B: FUNCTIONS OF COMMERCIAL BANKS (DETAILED & CLASSIFIED)
3. Classification of Bank Functions

Functions of commercial banks are broadly divided into:

• Primary Functions

• Secondary Functions

• Credit Creation (Unique Function)
4. Primary Functions of Commercial Banks
A. Acceptance of Deposits (FULL DETAIL)

Accepting deposits from the public is the first and most important function of commercial banks. Deposits constitute the main source of funds for banks. Banks encourage people to save by providing safety of money, liquidity and interest.

Types of Deposits (Explained Individually):



1. Savings Deposit Account:

This account is designed to encourage saving habits among individuals. It earns moderate interest and allows limited withdrawals.



2. Current Deposit Account:

This account is mainly used by businessmen and firms for frequent transactions. It provides high liquidity but does not earn interest.



3. Fixed Deposit Account:

In this account, money is deposited for a fixed period of time. It earns higher interest and is suitable for long-term savings.



4. Recurring Deposit Account:

In this account, a fixed amount is deposited regularly, usually every month. It promotes disciplined saving among people with regular income.
B. Lending of Money (FULL DETAIL)

The second primary function of banks is lending money. Banks lend money out of the deposits collected from the public. Lending generates income for banks in the form of interest and supports economic activities.

Forms of Loans and Advances:



• Term Loans: Provided for long-term purposes such as housing, education or machinery purchase.

• Cash Credit: Short-term credit facility mainly for business operations.

• Overdraft: Facility that allows customers to withdraw more than their deposit balance.

• Discounting of Bills: Banks provide immediate cash against bills of exchange.
5. Secondary Functions of Commercial Banks
A. Agency Functions (Very Detailed)
PART C: CREDIT CREATION BY COMMERCIAL BANKS (CORE CONCEPT)

Banks perform agency functions on behalf of their customers. These include collection of cheques, dividends and interest, payment of utility bills, taxes and insurance premiums, and acting as trustees, executors or representatives.
B. Utility Functions (Very Detailed)

Banks also provide several general utility services such as locker facilities, ATM services, debit cards, credit cards, internet banking, mobile banking, foreign exchange services and remittance facilities.
PART C: CREDIT CREATION BY COMMERCIAL BANKS (CORE  CONCEPT)
6. Meaning of Credit Creation

Credit creation refers to the ability of commercial banks to create multiple deposits by lending more than the actual cash reserves maintained by them. This is a unique and powerful function of banks.

Banks keep only a small fraction of total deposits as cash reserve and lend the remaining amount. The lent amount again becomes deposits in the banking system, leading to a chain reaction of deposit creation.
7. Limitations of Credit Creation (Fully Explained)

Credit creation by banks is subject to several limitations:



• Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) prescribed by RBI

• Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)

• Availability of credit demand in the economy

• Banking habits of the public

• Monetary policy measures of RBI

blocks.content: PART D: TYPES OF BANKS IN INDIA (EXHAUSTIVE COVERAGE)
8. Commercial Banks
Commercial banks provide banking services to the general public and business firms. They operate with profit motive.
9. Public Sector Banks
Public sector banks are owned and controlled by the Government of India. They play a major role in financial inclusion and development. Example: State Bank of India.
10. Private Sector Banks
Private sector banks are owned by private individuals or companies. They operate with profit motive and focus on efficiency.
11. Cooperative Banks
Cooperative banks are organised on cooperative principles and aim to provide affordable credit to members, especially in rural areas.
12. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)
RRBs were established to provide banking services in rural and semi-urban areas. They focus on farmers, artisans, small entrepreneurs and weaker sections.
PART E: NATIONALISATION OF BANKS IN INDIA
13. Meaning of Nationalisation of Banks

items: Be prepared to distinguish between Primary Functions (Deposits, Lending) and Secondary Functions (Agency, Utility) of commercial banks.
Understand the theoretical mechanics and practical limitations of Credit Creation by commercial banks.
Memorize the key objectives and socioeconomic rationale behind Bank Nationalisation in India.
Differentiate between the target beneficiaries and regulatory frameworks of Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Cooperative Banks.

blocks.content: Nationalisation of banks refers to the transfer of ownership and control of private banks to the government to serve public interest.
14. Objectives of Bank Nationalisation

• Expansion of banking facilities in rural areas

• Financial inclusion of weaker sections

• Priority sector lending

• Reduction of regional imbalance

• Support to planned economic development
PART F: ROLE OF BANKS IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
15. Role of Banks (Exhaustively Explained)

Banks contribute to economic development by mobilising savings, promoting capital formation, financing agriculture and industry, supporting trade and commerce, generating employment and stabilising the economy.
HIGHEST LEVEL FINAL REVISION POINTS

• Banks mobilise savings and promote investment

• Deposits are the main source of bank funds

• Lending supports economic activities

• Credit creation is a unique function

• RBI regulates credit creation

• RRBs strengthen rural economy
